title: The nine ways of prayer
hookLine: an early book shows Dominic praying with his whole body: bowing, lying prostrate, standing, reading

lines: A BOOK OPEN ON HIS KNEES.
cards: Dominic left no handbook on how he prayed. What survives is better, in a way: a record of what people saw. Late at night in a church, a man bows low before the altar.
Later he's flat on the stone floor, face down. Later still he's on his feet, arms stretched wide, then reaching straight up, as if for something just out of reach.

Then he sits with a book open on his knees and talks to it, nodding, sometimes smiling. The brothers noticed. An early little book gathered it all and named it: the nine ways of prayer of Saint Dominic.
Today, prayer that doesn't stay in the head.

teach.b: Walk through the ways the little book describes. He bows deeply, as you'd bow to someone you honor. He lies face down, the posture of someone with nothing left to offer but himself.
He kneels and stands and kneels again, like a person knocking at a door.

teach.h: HANDS OPEN LIKE A BOOK; ARMS LIKE A CROSS.
teach.b: He stands with his hands open before him, as if reading from a book. He stretches his arms out like a cross. He reaches up high.
He sits and reads quietly, as if in conversation.

teach.h: SITTING WITH A BOOK; WALKING THE ROAD.
teach.b: And walking from town to town, he prays as he goes. The book ties these postures to scripture, and the Psalms are full of them.

In the Douay-Rheims: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice." Lifted hands, noticed by God. Why would a preacher, a man of words, pray so much with his body?
The idea under the little book, in substance, runs both ways: the soul moves the body, and the body in turn stirs the soul. Kneel and you remember you're small.

teach.h: THE LIFTING UP OF MY HANDS.
teach.b: Open your hands and you remember you're receiving. Catholics still do something like this at Mass: standing for the Gospel, kneeling at the consecration, bowing during the Creed.
Dominic just did it alone, at night, with no one watching. Except someone was.

how: Catholics pray with posture at Mass, standing for the Gospel, kneeling at the consecration and bowing in the Creed; Dominicans still read and teach the early book on the ways Saint Dominic prayed.

games.q: what does “the nine ways of prayer” mean?
o: nine rules Dominic set for keeping silence at night
an early record of Dominic praying with his whole body
nine prayers Dominic wrote for the rosary's beads

games.q: the ways he prayed — tap the pairs.
p: hands open in front of him
as if reading from a book

s: Dominic wrote the nine ways down himself
an early little book written by others gathers what people saw him do.
one of the ways is sitting quietly and reading
he read as if in conversation, sometimes nodding or smiling.
the Psalms already pray with the body
'the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice.'

games.q: you're a young friar. you want to learn to pray like Dominic, but he has written nothing about how he prays. what do you do?
o: ask him for his method in writing.
watch how he prays, and write down what you see.
wait for him to preach a sermon on it.
games.why: that's what survives: an early little book of what people saw, bowing, lying flat, arms wide, reading, walking. prayer learned by watching.

practice: Pick a posture you don't usually use: stand with your hands open in front of you, palms up, like an open book, or kneel, or if you're sitting, lift your hands a little from your lap.

Stay with it and notice what it does, how open hands feel different from folded ones; if you pray, let the posture be the prayer, perhaps with the psalm's line about lifted hands, and if not, just breathe and notice how your body holds the moment.

wordCard.voice: The nine ways of prayer. An early book's record of Dominic praying with his whole body: bowing, lying flat, standing, reaching, reading, walking. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a way of praying. the early book describes Dominic's ways of prayer, one posture at a time.

carryVoice: Your line: the body prays. Nine ways, and not one of them stayed in the head. That's today, done.
